transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-19
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jorge Martinez (OptimaData VP Eng), Leah Kim (OptimaData SRE), Sam Patel (OptimaData ML Eng)
Shared links: Benchmark spreadsheet (drive.google.com/drive/fake-link), Security FAQ (redwood.com/sec-faq)

Summary: quick review of last week's benchmark runs; looked at latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput (req/s and tokens/s) comparing Redwood hosted and the customer's baseline provider; discussed tuning (batching, kv cache, quantization) and next steps to move to a short dedicated trial and deeper private networking check.

Topics covered:
- Baseline numbers vs Redwood runs
- p95/p99 tail latency and outliers during concurrency spikes
- Batching strategy impact on cost and latency
- KV/prefix cache hits and TTLs
- Quantization vs quality tradeoffs (int8/4-bit)
- Dedicated capacity trial and networking/SOC2 questions

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Jorge Martinez: Jorge here.
[00:06] Leah Kim: Leah, on SRE.
[00:07] Sam Patel: Sam, ML.
[00:09] Priya Nair: Priya, SE from Redwood. Alex on the AE side.
[00:13] Alex Morgan: Cool. We blocked 45 minutes, we'll go through the benchmark sheet we shared and then tune recommendations. Priya you wanna kick off with the numbers?
[00:20] Priya Nair: Yeah sure. So the sheet - quick note: we ran two main workloads that mirror the samples you sent, Sam. One is the chat-like 512 token median with occasional 1,024 token tails, the other is the short completion flow ~64 tokens.
[00:35] Priya Nair: For the 512 median workload on the baseline provider your table shows p50 around 120ms per token and p95 around 420ms per token, with end-to-end p99 at around 1.2s for a 32-concurrency run. On Redwood hosted with the default config we measured p50 ~95ms/token, p95 ~280ms/token, p99 ~800ms — so roughly 30-40% improvement on median and ~35-40% on tails in these runs.
[01:00] Sam Patel: Is that for H100 backends on Redwood? I just wanna make sure we're comparing apples to apples - baseline is their managed instance on A100s.
[01:08] Priya Nair: Good call. Baseline was A100. For the Redwood numbers we used H100 and a tuned kernel set; we also tested with A100 config and saw about 8-10% difference versus H100, so still a net win on our tuned runtime.
[01:22] Jorge Martinez: Can you clarify tokens per second throughput at 32 concurrency? We saw a drop-off on the baseline after burst.
[01:29] Priya Nair: Sure - at steady state on the 512 token median, baseline averaged ~220 tokens/s/core (aggregate across instances) whereas Redwood aggregated ~320 tokens/s under the same concurrency, which is why latency tails are better — fewer queuing effects.
[01:45] Leah Kim: We noticed some p99 spikes overnight in your runs — are those tied to autoscaling events? We need stable tails for our SLA.
[01:52] Priya Nair: There were two categories. One was autoscaler warm-up on the baseline provider where scale-up created request queuing. On Redwood hosted we used continuous batching and pre-warming which reduced warm-up spikes. The second was KV cache misses during rare long prefix sequences — if the cache TTL was short we saw cold-starts at p99.
[02:15] Alex Morgan: Quick interjection — we added a small experiment in the sheet: recommended cache TTL of 30 minutes for conversational sessions reduces cold misses by ~78% on our trace.
[02:26] Sam Patel: That cache TTL sounds promising. Does that increase memory footprint a lot? Concerned about OOMs on smaller instances.
[02:33] Priya Nair: It's a trade. TTL increases memory but we use an LRU-sharded cache with eviction that keeps memory bounded. For your workload, with the session stickiness you described, expect less than a 10% memory footprint increase on the recommended dedicated pool.
[02:47] Jorge Martinez: Ok. Let's talk cost — how does the cost-per-1M tokens compare after tuning? Baseline vendor gave us a rate where with batching they get to $X per 1M but their latency degrades.
[02:58] Priya Nair: In the annotated sheet we included an apples-to-apples cost calc. After enabling 4-8 token packing batching and KV caching, Redwood's cost per 1M tokens for the 512 median workload was about 18% lower than baseline while keeping p95 latency under your 500ms target. If you push quantization to int8/4-bit you can reduce cost another ~12% but we'd want to run quality checks.
[03:22] Leah Kim: About quantization — we have compliance concerns and also want to make sure hallucination rate doesn't go up. What do you typically see?
[03:29] Priya Nair: For most LLMs in our catalog, int8 keeps quality similar for retrieval-augmented flows; int4 can sometimes introduce small regressions in open-ended generation. We always recommend running your eval prompts — we offered to run the eval set you already shared.
[03:44] Sam Patel: Did you run the eval we sent last week? Any red flags?
[03:47] Priya Nair: We ran the eval on both baseline and Redwood-tuned. Preliminary: no significant delta in F1/accuracy for your classification prompt set. We flagged a handful of edge cases in open ended responses for int4. Those are noted in the sheet under "quality notes".
[04:02] Alex Morgan: We'll attach those example mismatches in the sheet as well.
[04:06] Jorge Martinez: On dedicated vs hosted — our legal team prefers dedicated to ensure data isolation. We wanted to understand initial throughput guarantees and autoscale behavior.
[04:17] Priya Nair: For Dedicated we can provision a reserved GPU pool with steady-state guarantees. You can pick a min capacity and burst capacity. The autoscaler is configurable: we can do predictive warm pools to avoid cold starts. For SLAs we can commit uptime and p95 targets as part of the pilot.
[04:36] Leah Kim: Networking — for a short dedicated trial we'll need IP whitelisting and VPN peering. Can you support private VPC peering?
[04:44] Alex Morgan: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC peering and customer-managed networking. For hosted Dedicated we do IP allowlist and can negotiate a secure peering. We'll set up a private networking deep-dive next week with your SREs.
[04:58] Priya Nair: Also noted: Leah asked about audit logs retention. We support configurable retention; default is 90 days but can extend for enterprise. We'll include SOC2/ISO artifacts.
[05:10] Jorge Martinez: Great. A couple of specific questions on the benchmark itself — noise and run-to-run variance. We saw ~12% variance on baseline runs. What's your margin?
[05:19] Priya Nair: We run 10 replicate runs, drop the top and bottom 10% for noise, then report median and p95/p99. Our internal variance on the Redwood runs was about 4-6% after tuning, largely due to GPU scheduling and instance warm-up avoidance.
[05:34] Sam Patel: For the 1k token tails, how does batching behave? Does it push smaller requests behind?
[05:40] Priya Nair: Our batching is dynamic and grouping is by token length windows so small requests are not massively delayed. We also support priority lanes for low-latency requests — you can reserve a small percentage of capacity to keep them sub-100ms for short completions. That of course increases cost slightly.
[05:58] Jorge Martinez: Can we see an example config for the priority lane?
[06:00] Priya Nair: We'll put a snippet in the sheet — it's a simple route policy with min-allocated qps and a separate batch size cap.
[06:09] Alex Morgan: Back to the numbers, an important slide: the stress runs at 128 concurrency showed baseline had a queuing cliff where p99 jumped to 3.5s. Redwood stayed under ~1.1s in our test. Any idea why the baseline cliff happens?
[06:23] Sam Patel: That sounds like an autoscale or scheduler queuing effect — they've got cold workers coming up?
[06:27] Priya Nair: Exactly. Also kernel selection and memory fragmentation on their runtime caused some degradation. Our runtime does continuous batching and active KV cache amortization which smooths that cliff.
[06:38] Leah Kim: Real-world question, what's the onboarding for a dedicated trial? We have a two-week window to test before next quarter decisions.
[06:46] Alex Morgan: We can spin up a dedicated pool in 48-72 hours once network peering is validated. The trial would be two weeks with a defined test harness — we can run the baseline comparison and then let you run production-like traffic.
[06:58] Jorge Martinez: Ok timeline aligns. For the dedicated pool, will you provide the same H100 instance types?
[07:04] Priya Nair: Yes, you can pick H100 or A100 variants. For your load H100 gave best latency in our runs. We'll also offer an option to cap to A100 for cost parity.
[07:15] Sam Patel: One more on model variants — are you doing model distillation or smaller variants for lower latency?
[07:20] Priya Nair: We can serve distilled or quantized variants as needed; we also support routing to lighter models for specific routes. We tested a smaller 7B variant for short completions and it was sub-100ms p95 with acceptable accuracy on those specific prompts.
[07:36] Jorge Martinez: Any security showstoppers for us? Our legal wants SSO/SAML, token rotation, and KMS integration.
[07:44] Alex Morgan: All supported. SSO via SAML, RBAC, key management via customer KMS/HSM, and audit logs. We'll attach the security pack and a SOC2 attestation.
[07:56] Leah Kim: Good. A quick nit: some product names in the sheet are spelled weird — I think "Reedwood" in one tab — minor but confuses legal.
[08:03] Alex Morgan: Thanks — we'll clean that up.
[08:07] Priya Nair: Quick demo note: we also ran a run with quantization + cache + pack batching for 64-token flow and ended up reducing cost by ~34% vs baseline while keeping p95 under 80ms. The sheet has the exact config and cost calc.
[08:24] Sam Patel: Nice. Where are the raw logs? We wanna sanity-check latency distributions.
[08:28] Priya Nair: Raw runs and perf logs are in the drive link we shared; you'll find the per-request CSVs and aggregated dashboards.
[08:34] Jorge Martinez: Great. Any blockers to starting the dedicated trial this Friday?
[08:38] Alex Morgan: The main blocker is networking peering and IP allowlist from your side; also decision on H100 vs A100. If we get the trace and the IPs this week, we can be live by Monday.
[08:50] Leah Kim: I'll work with infra to get that.
[08:54] Sam Patel: Also confirm the eval prompts — we'll add 20 more edge-case prompts to the eval set by EOD tomorrow.
[08:59] Priya Nair: Perfect, we'll run them and return quality diffs.
[09:03] Alex Morgan: Anything else on the benchmark numbers?
[09:06] Jorge Martinez: One question — in the sheet there's a column called "pack rate" — explain that again.
[09:11] Priya Nair: Pack rate is average token packing per batch — e.g., how many tokens across requests were grouped into a single kernel execution. Higher pack rates improve throughput/cost but can increase latency for small requests unless priority lanes are used.
[09:25] Jorge Martinez: Ok. That's helpful.
[09:28] Alex Morgan: Alright sounds like we're agreed on next steps. Quick recap then we'll close.
[09:33] Priya Nair: Recap: Redwood to send cleaned benchmark sheet + config snippets, run the expanded eval prompts, provide recommended batching/ttl/json snippets; OptimaData to provide 48-hour trace and IP allowlist; schedule SRE deep-dive for networking the week of 6/29.
[09:48] Jorge Martinez: Yup. Thanks everyone.
[09:50] Leah Kim: Thanks.
[09:51] Sam Patel: Thanks.
[09:52] Alex Morgan: I'll follow up with the sheet and a calendar invite for the networking call.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional misheard product names and some dropped punctuation. The body contains filler words and cross-talk.

End of call.
